title: Digital Tools, Systems & Workplace Responsibility
summary: Learn how workplace digital tools support communication, information, planning, collaboration, and operations—and why responsible use includes following policies, protecting information, and respecting authorization boundaries.
objectives: Identify common categories of digital workplace tools and their purposes.
Explain why access to a tool does not automatically authorize every possible use.
Recognize basic responsibilities involving accounts, information, permissions, and digital conduct.

vocab.def: The collection of digital tools, systems, information, and communication channels used to perform work.
Permission to perform a particular action, access information, or use a system for an approved purpose.
The ability to enter, view, or use a digital system or resource.
Using workplace technology in a way that follows policy, protects information, respects permissions, and supports accurate work.

sections.heading: Digital tools are part of everyday work
sections.body: Workplaces may use email, messaging, calendars, documents, databases, customer systems, project tools, video meetings, AI assistants, specialized software, and other digital systems. Different tools support different responsibilities.

sections.heading: Access is not the same as authorization
sections.body: Being technically able to open a file, system, or feature does not automatically mean you are permitted to use it for every purpose. Workplace roles, policies, and permissions still determine what actions are appropriate.

sections.heading: Use the right system for the right purpose
sections.body: Moving information into an unapproved app, personal account, public tool, or informal channel can create privacy, security, ownership, or recordkeeping problems.

sections.heading: Digital conduct is professional conduct
sections.body: Messages, files, comments, edits, searches, uploads, and system actions can affect coworkers, customers, records, and organizational decisions. Professional standards still apply when work happens digitally.

practice.prompt: You can technically open a shared folder containing information unrelated to your role. Does your technical access automatically mean you should use the information?
practice.answer: No. Access does not automatically establish authorization or a legitimate workplace purpose.

practice.prompt: You want to move a work document into a personal online tool because it is easier to use. What should you consider first?
practice.answer: Check whether the tool and transfer are approved and whether the document contains private, sensitive, confidential, or restricted information.

quiz.question: Which statement best reflects responsible digital workplace behavior?
options: Use approved tools for authorized purposes and protect workplace information
If a system lets you do something, it is automatically permitted
Personal accounts are always acceptable for work files
Digital actions matter less than in-person actions
quiz.answer: Use approved tools for authorized purposes and protect workplace information

lab.objective: Review simulated digital workplace scenarios and decide whether each action is appropriate, requires clarification, should be avoided, or should be escalated.

reflectionPrompt: Why is being able to access a digital resource different from being authorized to use it?
